Cope's gray treefrog (Dryophytes chrysoscelis) is a relatively small hylid that exhibits a moderate lifespan for an anuran of its body size. Under stable laboratory conditions maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum recorded longevity extends to approximately 2,847 days [am = approximately 2,847 days]. This value, equivalent to roughly 7.8 years, places the species in an intermediate position among North American hylids, with a lifespan notably shorter than the 8 to 10 years reported for larger ranids but considerably exceeding that of many small-bodied chorus frogs. Such longevity is closely tied to the species' ability to persist in ephemeral breeding habitats and its reliance on seasonal cues for reproductive activation.

A particularly informative aspect of the species' early life history is the duration of the embryonic period under controlled thermal conditions. When eggs are incubated at a constant 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the interval from oviposition to the hatching event spans 21 days [ab = 21 days]. This developmental timeline is consistent with expectations for temperate-zone hylids, where cooler incubation temperatures extend the period of embryonic dependency on internal yolk reserves. At birth, each newly hatched tadpole emerges at a very modest wet weight of approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value that represents a tiny fraction of the ultimate adult mass and reflects the energetically constrained nature of the yolk-laden egg from which it hatches.

Following successful emergence from the egg, the free-swimming tadpole enters an extended period of exogenous feeding and somatic growth before undergoing the dramatic anatomical restructuring characteristic of anuran metamorphosis. Under the same thermally favorable regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the duration from the hatching event to the completion of metamorphosis is 49 days . This larval period, measured as time since birth, is a critical life-history variable that influences both juvenile survival and the timing of the terrestrial transition. The allometric shift during metamorphic climax is energetically demanding, and the length of this larval stage is highly sensitive to local variations in temperature and resource availability.

Ultimately, female Cope's gray treefrogs attain a maximum adult body mass of 5.47 grams [Wwi = 5.47 grams], a value representing the asymptotic wet weight for reproductively active individuals. Following metamorphosis, females undergo a prolonged period of juvenile growth before reaching sexual maturity. Under standard conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the time since metamorphosis at which puberty is attained is 730 days [tp = 730 days]. This extended maturation period, spanning approximately two years, is a significant investment that allows females to accumulate sufficient energetic reserves to support the high energetic demands of subsequent egg production and amplexus.

Reproductive activity in this species is seasonal and closely tied to warm, wet conditions that favor egg mass deposition and tadpole development. At 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females achieve their maximum reproductive rate by producing approximately 2.74 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.74 clutches per year]. Each clutch contains a consistent number of eggs, with field studies recording an average of 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = 1 egg per clutch]. The resting metabolic rate, measured as basal oxygen consumption in post-absorptive adult females, was found to be 0.0116 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0116 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], providing a baseline reference for understanding the species' comparatively low energetic demands.
